messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Over-Conservative Adaptation
parts:
As Ben first brought up a few months ago the step size adaptation seems to be
way too conservative, at least for simple models. For example, setting he target
average acceptance probability to 0.8 can yield an empirical average of 0.9, and
setting the target to 0.7 can yield an empirical average of 0.8.

This was really annoying for the workshop where all we had were simple models,
so I decided to take a deeper look into what might be going on, and here’s my
best guess.

Recall that the symplectic integrators we use are well-behaved up to some step size
where they diverge. Let’s call that step size epsilon_bad. In a complex model the
optimal step size will be way below epsilon_bad, ave_accept_prob(epsilon) will be
roughly symmetric, and the Nesterov dual average works well.

On the other hand, in a simple model the optimal step size can be right up against the
divergence threshold. In a simple Gaussian, for example, the step size isn’t limited
by the stable error but by the divergence. This manifests as ave_accept_prob(epsilon)
being highly skewed, with a rapid divergence between the optimal step size and
epsilon_bad. Consequently the dual average creeps up to the optimal step size
from below until it passes it and starts to diverge. The divergences induce a correction
that pushes the test value to much smaller values at which point the dual average
begins to creep up again.

Basically this behavior cycles repeatedly, converging only veeeeeeery slowly to the
optimal value. The most likely outcome is ending up below the optimal step size (with
too high of an optimal acceptance probability) and increasing the terminal buffer (where
we learn the final step size) doesn’t really do anything because the convergence is
so slow.

In other words, in simple models ave_accept_prob(epsilon) doesn’t look all that
quadratic and the convergence of the dual averaging suffers accordingly. Anyone
have any thoughts? Should we be satisfied with this behavior or try to generalize
our adaptation to identify this situation and respond accordingly?

-Mike

messages.author: 1004dd6f66bb10c3
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Over-Conservative Adaptation
parts:
This is an interesting question. I think I agree with the diagnosis, although it's a little surprising to me that the divergence is extreme, since the updates should be bounded.

I wonder if AdaGrad would work better.

If we wanted to get *really* fancy, we could use some kind of Gaussian process-based Bayesian optimization. That would definitely solve this problem, since we'd be approximating the function accept_rate(ε) by something much more powerful than a combination of noisy linear approximations. And after all, if we're Bayesians why are we using frequentist online optimization procedures?* 

If we went down that road, we could also swap out acceptance rates for (expected squared jump distance)/(expected number of steps), which acceptance rate is arguably just a proxy for.

Matt

* Answer: probably the same reason we use a frequentist procedure like Monte Carlo approximation.

geometric perspective — paper coming as soon as we see where the geometry of HMC paper
goes first.

messages.author: a236d3d356ca53fd
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Over-Conservative Adaptation
parts: > If we wanted to get *really* fancy, we could use some kind of Gaussian process-based Bayesian optimization. That would definitely solve this problem, since we'd be approximating the function accept_rate(ε) by something much more powerful than a combination of noisy linear approximations.

I assume that the function is unimodal, in which case it would probably be more efficient and simpler to use some parametric form taking into account the skewness and the divergent behavior on the other side of the model. The generic Gaussian process prior would be too flexible, but unimodal GP prior with additional functional constraints and input dependent noise model would be *really* fancy.

Aki

Here is an example where this behavior occurs but the model, while Gaussian, is not so simple. Basically, there is a regression function for the mean vector, an LKJ thing with some standard deviations for the covariance matrix, and 1754 * 3 multivariate normal latents.

We see the odd combination of lots of divergence early and late in warmup but none after warmup. It looks like it might be doing okay from iteration 2000 to 3500, but then it hits the last 50 iterations of warmup and diverges a lot in that subwindow. And it fails all the convergence monitoring in the post-warmup period.
